tools.title: Summary statistics
tools.useWhen: You need the mean, median, standard deviation, five-number summary, or IQR.
steps: Choose the Single Variable tab. Under Enter Data, select Your Own.
Select Individual Observations if you have a list of data values.
Enter the variable name and paste your observations into the entry box.
Read the Descriptive Statistics table for the mean, standard deviation, five-number summary, and IQR.
tools.interpret: Identify the center and spread, and explain what they mean in the units of your variable.

screenshots.alt: Quantitative data app with Your Own data and Individual Observations selected. The descriptive statistics table reports n = 27, mean 67,648, sample standard deviation 27,676, minimum 25,000, Q1 40,000, median 64,000, Q3 85,000, maximum 140,000, and IQR 45,000; a histogram and boxplot appear beside it.
screenshots.caption: Example calculator screen. Your assignment’s data and settings may differ.

tools.keywords: five number summary quartiles median mean standard deviation IQR S6

tools.title: Histograms, boxplots & dotplots
tools.useWhen: You want to visualize the distribution of a quantitative variable.
steps: Under Enter Data, select Your Own and choose Individual Observations for a list of data values.
Enter the variable name and paste your observations into the entry box.
Under Choose Type of Plot, check Histogram, Boxplot, or Dotplot as needed. Stem & Leaf is also available.
For a histogram, adjust Select Binwidth for Histogram if your assignment asks for a particular bin width.
tools.interpret: Describe shape, center, spread, and any unusual values. Check the axis labels and units.

screenshots.alt: Quantitative data app with Histogram, Boxplot, Dotplot, and Stem & Leaf selected, showing all four displays for 27 observations.
screenshots.caption: Example calculator screen. Your assignment’s data and settings may differ.

tools.keywords: histogram box plot dot plot numeric numerical

tools.title: Bar graphs & frequency tables
tools.useWhen: Your observations are categories and you want counts or proportions.
steps: Choose the One Categorical Variable tab.
Under Enter Data, select Individual Observations when entering category labels.
Enter the variable name, then paste category labels into the observations box; the app accepts observations separated by spaces or pasted from a spreadsheet column.
Read the Frequency Table and Bar Graph. Plot Percent changes the graph from counts to percentages.
tools.interpret: Explain which categories are most common and whether you are comparing counts or proportions.

screenshots.alt: One Categorical Variable tab with Individual Observations selected. The frequency table and bar graph show no: 25, yes: 9, and maybe: 5, for a total of 39 observations; Pareto Chart is checked.
screenshots.caption: Example calculator screen. Your assignment’s data and settings may differ.

tools.courseNote: The example has Pareto Chart checked, which orders bars by frequency. Use the bar-chart settings requested in your assignment.
tools.inputs: Category labels or category counts, as requested by the app.

tools.title: Expected value
tools.useWhen: You have a discrete probability distribution and need its long-run mean.
tools.appName: Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean (Discrete Population)
tools.location: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem
steps: Under Select Population Distribution, choose Build Custom Distribution.
Enter the Number of distinct values (the number of possible outcomes).
Double-click or double-tap each table cell to enter the outcomes x and probabilities P(x). Check that Total equals 1.
Read the population mean μ above the Population Distribution graph; this is the expected value. The graph also shows the population standard deviation σ.
tools.interpret: The expected value is the long-run average over many repetitions; it need not be a possible single outcome.

screenshots.alt: Custom discrete distribution with outcomes 1 through 5 and probabilities 0.230, 0.110, 0.110, 0.130, and 0.420, totaling 1. The population graph shows mean 3.4 and standard deviation 1.64.
screenshots.caption: Example calculator screen. Your assignment’s data and settings may differ.

tools.courseNote: For expected value, use the population mean above the graph. You do not need to click Draw Sample(s); the sample-size and simulation controls serve a different task. Probabilities must be between 0 and 1 and total 1. The original guide notes that calculations may take 30 seconds or more.
tools.inputs: The possible outcomes x and their probabilities P(x).
tools.keywords: expected value discrete probability distribution mean E(x)

tools.title: Binomial probabilities
tools.useWhen: You count successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability.
steps: Choose Find Probabilities.
Enter the number of trials n and success probability p.
Enter x and choose the inequality that matches the question.
tools.interpret: Translate the result into a sentence about the number of successes. Check whether the question says exactly, at least, or at most.

screenshots.alt: Binomial distribution app tabs, including Find Probabilities.

tools.inputs: Number of trials n, success probability p, and success count x.
tools.keywords: binomial exactly at least at most successes

tools.title: Normal probabilities
tools.useWhen: You know a value or interval and want the probability or area for a normal distribution.
steps: Choose Find Probability.
Enter the mean and standard deviation.
Select the probability type (below, above, or between) and enter the boundary value or values.
tools.interpret: The shaded area represents the probability. Describe that area using the variable and units from the problem.

screenshots.alt: Normal probability controls showing mean, standard deviation, probability type, and a boundary value x.

tools.courseNote: For the standard normal distribution, use mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1.
tools.inputs: Mean, standard deviation, and boundary value or values.
tools.keywords: normal probability z score area below above between

tools.title: Normal percentiles & quartiles
tools.useWhen: You know a percentage or probability and want the corresponding value in a normal distribution.
steps: Choose Find Percentile/Quantile.
Enter the mean and standard deviation.
Choose the percentile type and enter the probability in the format requested by the app.
tools.interpret: The output is a cutoff value. State what percentage lies below or above it, using the tail you selected.

screenshots.alt: Normal percentile controls showing mean, standard deviation, Lower Tail, and a probability field labeled in percent.

tools.courseNote: For the standard normal distribution, use mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1. Check whether the input field requests a percent (95) or a decimal (0.95).
tools.inputs: Mean, standard deviation, and the desired percentile or tail probability.

tools.title: One-mean t-interval
tools.useWhen: You estimate a population mean using one sample and an unknown population standard deviation.
steps: Choose the Confidence Interval & Significance Test tab.
Select the Enter Data option appropriate to your assignment and enter the sample information. The screenshot uses a built-in textbook example.
Under Type of Inference, select Confidence Interval.
For a usual two-sided interval, select Two-Sided under Bounds; use another choice only if your assignment requests it.
Enter the assigned Confidence Level (%) as a percentage, such as 95 for 95%.
Read the Lower Bound and Upper Bound in the Confidence Interval table.
tools.interpret: Interpret the interval as an estimate of the population mean, in the units of the variable.

screenshots.alt: Inference for a Population Mean with Confidence Interval, Two-Sided bounds, and 95 percent confidence selected. The Airbnb example has n = 50, sample mean 105.94 dollars, sample standard deviation 56.40 dollars, and confidence interval 89.91 to 121.97 dollars.
screenshots.caption: Example calculator screen. Your assignment’s data and settings may differ.

tools.courseNote: The screenshot demonstrates the settings with a built-in Airbnb dataset. Replace that example with your assignment’s sample. Its displayed 95% interval is $89.91 to $121.97.
tools.inputs: Sample data or sample mean, sample standard deviation, sample size, and confidence level.
tools.keywords: one sample t interval confidence mean

tools.title: One-proportion z-interval
tools.useWhen: You estimate one population proportion from sample successes and a sample size.
steps: Choose Confidence Interval & Significance Test.
Enter the number of successes and sample size.
Choose the confidence level and WALD interval method.
tools.interpret: Interpret the interval as an estimate of the population proportion in context.

screenshots.alt: Inference for a population proportion app with a Confidence Interval & Significance Test tab.

tools.courseNote: For this course: use WALD for the interval method.
tools.inputs: Number of successes, sample size, and confidence level.
tools.keywords: one proportion confidence z interval Wald

tools.title: Two-proportion z-interval
tools.useWhen: You estimate the difference between two population proportions using independent samples.
tools.location: Confidence Intervals & Tests Comparing Two Groups
steps: Open Compare Two Proportions.
Use the linked video for the two-proportion interval procedure.
Enter both samples and select WALD for the interval method.
tools.interpret: Interpret the interval for the difference in proportions. Keep the group order consistent when explaining a positive or negative difference.
tools.courseNote: For this course: use WALD for the interval method.
tools.inputs: Success counts and sample sizes for both groups, plus a confidence level.
tools.keywords: two proportions confidence interval difference Wald

tools.title: One-proportion z-test
tools.useWhen: You test a claim about one population proportion.
steps: Open Inference for a Proportion.
Enter the sample information and hypothesized proportion.
Select the alternative hypothesis and SCORE test method; follow the linked example.
tools.interpret: Compare the p-value with the assigned significance level, then state what the evidence says about the claim.
tools.courseNote: For this course: use SCORE for the test method.
tools.inputs: Success count, sample size, null proportion, alternative hypothesis, and significance level.
tools.keywords: one proportion hypothesis z test Score

tools.title: Two-proportion z-test
tools.useWhen: You test whether two population proportions differ using independent samples.
tools.location: Confidence Intervals & Tests Comparing Two Groups
steps: Open Compare Two Proportions.
Enter both groups and select the alternative hypothesis.
Select SCORE for the test method; follow the linked example.
tools.interpret: Use the p-value to evaluate evidence of a difference. Name the groups and preserve their order.
tools.courseNote: For this course: use SCORE for the test method.
tools.inputs: Success counts and sample sizes for both groups, alternative hypothesis, and significance level.

tools.title: Independent two-sample t-test
tools.useWhen: You compare population means for two independent groups.
tools.location: Confidence Intervals & Tests Comparing Two Groups
steps: Choose Confidence Interval & Significance Test.
Enter the two independent samples using the available input option.
Select the alternative hypothesis and follow the linked example.
tools.interpret: Use the p-value to evaluate evidence of a difference between population means. Keep the group order and units clear.

screenshots.alt: Compare Two Population Means app tabs for Confidence Interval & Significance Test and Two Dependent Samples.

tools.inputs: Two independent samples or their summary statistics, plus the assigned test settings.
tools.keywords: independent two sample t test means

tools.title: Matched / paired t-test
tools.useWhen: You compare two measurements from the same people or explicitly matched pairs.
tools.location: Confidence Intervals & Tests Comparing Two Groups
steps: Choose Two Dependent Samples.
Enter the matched measurements, keeping each pair aligned.
Follow the paired t-test video and use the assigned alternative hypothesis.
tools.interpret: Interpret the test in terms of the population mean of the paired differences. Define which measurement is subtracted from which.

screenshots.alt: Compare Two Population Means app with the Two Dependent Samples tab for paired data.

tools.inputs: Two matched columns of quantitative measurements.
tools.keywords: matched paired dependent before after t test

tools.title: Chi-square goodness-of-fit
tools.useWhen: You compare observed counts for one categorical variable with a claimed distribution.
steps: Open Chi-Squared Test.
Use the linked video for the goodness-of-fit procedure.
Enter observed category counts and the expected distribution requested by the app.
tools.interpret: Use the p-value to evaluate whether the category distribution differs from the claimed distribution.
tools.inputs: Observed category counts and hypothesized category proportions or expected counts.
tools.keywords: chi square goodness of fit GOF one categorical

tools.title: Chi-square test of independence
tools.useWhen: You examine whether two categorical variables are associated.
steps: Open Chi-Squared Test.
Use the independence-test example that matches your data format.
Enter the two-way table or data as demonstrated in the video.
tools.interpret: Use the p-value to evaluate evidence of an association. An association alone does not establish cause and effect.
tools.inputs: Counts in a two-way table, or categorical data using the format in the video.
tools.keywords: chi square independence association two categorical contingency table

tools.title: One-way ANOVA
tools.useWhen: You compare population means across three or more independent groups.
steps: Open ANOVA (One-Way).
Use the linked video to enter the group data.
Run the analysis using your assignment’s settings.
tools.interpret: A significant result provides evidence that not all population means are equal. It does not by itself tell you which groups differ.
tools.inputs: Quantitative measurements with their group labels.

tools.title: Linear regression
tools.useWhen: You model the relationship between two quantitative variables or predict y from x.
steps: Choose Fit Linear Regression Model.
Enter paired x and y observations and identify the explanatory and response variables.
Read the fitted equation and follow the linked example.
tools.interpret: Explain the slope in context and use the model only where it is appropriate. A relationship alone does not establish causation.

screenshots.alt: Linear Regression app with Fit Linear Regression Model and Fitted Values & Residual Analysis tabs.

tools.inputs: Paired quantitative observations for x and y.
